name: The Iliad
author: Homer

claims.text: The Iliad covers roughly fifty days in the final year of the siege of Troy.
Its formulaic diction reflects oral compositional technique.
It reached approximately its present form in the 8th or 7th century BC.
Some described objects reflect genuine Bronze Age material culture.
A single poet composed the Iliad and the Odyssey.

milestones.text: Tradition credits Peisistratid Athens with fixing a standard written text for recital at the Panathenaia.
Earliest surviving copies: papyrus fragments from Ptolemaic Egypt.
Alexandrian scholars, above all Aristarchus, edit the text that later readers inherit.
The Venetus A, the oldest complete manuscript, preserves the Alexandrian scholars' notes in its margins.
First printed edition of Homer, edited by Demetrios Chalkokondyles in Florence.

summary: Fifty-one days in the tenth year of the Trojan War, framed entirely by the rage of Achilles and its consequences.
significance: The first and most influential work of European literature: the poem through which Greeks of every later age understood heroism, war and the gods.
body:
An epic of about 15,700 lines of hexameter verse in 24 books, the Iliad was composed around 750–700 BC, probably in Ionia on the coast of Asia Minor. Tradition credits it to Homer. Its repeated phrases — "swift-footed Achilles", "rosy-fingered Dawn" — are the tools of oral poets who composed as they performed, as Milman Parry showed in the 1930s by recording singers in the Balkans who still worked the same way.

It is not the story of the whole Trojan War. It covers about fifty days in the tenth year of the siege, and its subject is named in its first word: *mēnis*, wrath. Achilles quarrels with Agamemnon over a captive woman and withdraws from the fighting. His friend Patroclus is killed by the Trojan prince Hector, and Achilles returns to kill Hector and drag his body behind his chariot. The poem ends not with the fall of Troy but with Priam, Hector's father, coming alone to Achilles' tent to ransom his son's body, and the two enemies weeping together.

The story is set in the Bronze Age, and some of the objects it describes, such as the boar's-tusk helmet, are genuinely Mycenaean. But much of its world — its weapons, burials and politics — belongs to the poet's own centuries, making it a blend of remembered past and Archaic present.

Probably written down by the 6th century BC and later edited by scholars at Alexandria, it became the core of Greek education for a thousand years.

name: The Odyssey
author: Homer

claims.text: The Odyssey reached approximately its present form in the late 8th or early 7th century BC.
It was composed somewhat later than the Iliad.
Its formulaic diction reflects a tradition of oral composition in performance.
The Odyssey employs a non-linear narrative structure with embedded first-person narration.
The same poet composed the Iliad and the Odyssey.
Odysseus' voyages can be mapped to real Mediterranean locations.

milestones.text: Tradition credits Peisistratid Athens with fixing a standard written text for recital at the Panathenaia.
Earliest surviving copies: papyrus fragments from Ptolemaic Egypt.
Alexandrian scholars, above all Aristarchus, edit the text that later readers inherit.
Oldest complete copies: Byzantine manuscripts, from which every modern text descends.
First printed edition of Homer, edited by Demetrios Chalkokondyles in Florence.

summary: Odysseus' ten-year journey home from Troy, and the reclaiming of a household that has almost given him up.
significance: With the Iliad, the founding work of Greek literature: the model for every later story of a journey home, and the fullest picture of household, hospitality and status in early Greek society.
body:
An epic of about 12,100 lines of hexameter verse in 24 books, the Odyssey was composed around 725–675 BC, probably in the eastern Aegean, and probably somewhat later than the Iliad. Ancient tradition credits both poems to Homer; whether one poet made both is still debated. It grew out of centuries of oral poetry, and its repeated phrases — "rosy-fingered Dawn", "the wine-dark sea" — are the working toolkit of singers who composed as they performed.

The story begins near its end. Ten years after the fall of Troy, Odysseus is held on the island of Ogygia while suitors occupy his house on Ithaca and court his wife, Penelope. The first four books follow his son Telemachus; Odysseus then reaches the Phaeacians and tells his own wanderings — the Cyclops, Circe, the land of the dead, the Sirens — as a flashback. The second half is set on Ithaca, where he returns in disguise, tests his household and kills the suitors.

Where the Iliad is about glory in war, the Odyssey is about survival, cunning and home. Its hero is introduced as *polytropos*, "of many turns", and is admired for his lies. Its world of households, sea voyages and guest-friendship (*xenia*) between hosts and strangers belongs more to the poet's own age of trade and colonisation than to the Bronze Age in which the story is set.

The poem reached its fixed form through Athenian recitation and Alexandrian editing, and has shaped storytelling ever since, from Virgil's *Aeneid* to James Joyce's *Ulysses*.

name: Theogony
author: Hesiod

claims.text: The Theogony traces divine genealogy from Chaos to the rule of Zeus.
Its succession myth structurally parallels Hittite and Babylonian narratives.
It contains the earliest full accounts of Prometheus and Pandora.
The poem opens with an unusual first-person account of Hesiod's own encounter with the Muses on Mount Helicon.

milestones.text: Survives through Byzantine manuscripts, supplemented by ancient papyrus fragments from Egypt.
First printed by Aldus Manutius in Venice, in a volume with Theocritus.

summary: The genealogy of the gods from Chaos to the reign of Zeus — Greek religion's closest thing to a systematic cosmogony.
significance: The fullest early account of how the Greeks imagined the origins of the world and the gods, and key evidence for Near Eastern influence on Greek myth.
body:
A hexameter poem of about 1,000 lines, composed around 730–700 BC by Hesiod, a farmer-poet from Ascra in Boeotia. It opens unusually in the poet's own voice: the Muses appear to Hesiod as he tends sheep on Mount Helicon and give him the gift of song.

The poem traces the gods by generation. First come Chaos, Gaia (Earth) and Eros; then Ouranos (Sky), who imprisons his children until Gaia arms their son Kronos to castrate him. Kronos swallows his own children to keep power, until Zeus, hidden at birth, overthrows him and the Titans. Power passes by violence three times before Zeus establishes a lasting order. Along the way the poem gives the earliest full accounts of Prometheus stealing fire and of Pandora, the first woman, sent as punishment.

This succession story closely parallels the Hittite *Song of Kumarbi* and the Babylonian *Enuma Elish*, which also tell of generations of gods overthrown by their sons. The parallels are among the clearest evidence that early Greek myth drew on the older cultures of the Near East.

Alongside Homer, the Theogony became the standard reference for Greek gods' family relationships, and it is the main source behind most modern retellings of Greek creation myth.

name: Works and Days
author: Hesiod

claims.text: Works and Days is addressed to Hesiod's brother in an inheritance dispute.
It contains detailed practical instruction on farming and craft.
It presents the myth of five successive declining ages.
It is the earliest surviving Greek poem with an identified personal narrator.

milestones.text: Survives through Byzantine manuscripts, supplemented by ancient papyrus fragments from Egypt.
First printed in Milan with the Idylls of Theocritus.

summary: A farming almanac addressed to the poet's dishonest brother — and the first personal voice in European literature.
significance: The best early source for ordinary farming life in Greece, and the first poem in European literature spoken in a named poet's own voice.
body:
A hexameter poem of about 830 lines, composed around 700 BC by Hesiod of Ascra in Boeotia, author of the Theogony. It is addressed to his brother Perses, who had bribed the local "gift-devouring" lords to take more than his share of their father's farm.

The poem mixes moral argument with practical advice. It urges honest work and justice, telling the myth of Prometheus and Pandora and the myth of the Five Ages — gold, silver, bronze, heroes and iron — each worse than the last, down to Hesiod's own harsh present. It then becomes a farmer's calendar: when to plough, sow and harvest by the rising of the stars, how to build a plough, when it is safe to sail. It ends with the "Days", a list of which days of the month are lucky or unlucky for each task.

Unlike Homer, Hesiod speaks as himself. He names his village, describes his father's move from Asia Minor, and complains about the weather and his neighbours. That personal voice, and the picture of small-scale farming under local aristocrats, make the poem a unique window on rural life in the early Archaic period.

Virgil's *Georgics* took it as its model, and its Five Ages became Western culture's classic image of decline from a golden age.

name: The Homeric Hymns
author: Various, anonymous

claims.text: The Homeric Hymns use Homeric metre and dialect but are not by Homer.
The Hymn to Demeter is the principal early source for the Persephone myth.
They were probably performed as preludes to longer epic recitation.
The individual hymns vary widely in date, some possibly as late as the sixth or fifth century BC, making the collection a composite rather than a single work.

milestones.text: Survive only in late Byzantine manuscripts, usually copied with other early hexameter poetry.
Printed with the first edition of Homer in Florence.
Christian Friedrich Matthaei finds the only manuscript of the Hymn to Demeter in Moscow.

summary: Thirty-three hexameter hymns to individual gods — preludes to epic recitation, and the fullest early narratives of several myths.
significance: The fullest early tellings of several central myths, including Demeter and Persephone, the charter story of the Eleusinian Mysteries.
body:
A collection of 33 hexameter poems addressed to individual gods, composed by different, anonymous poets mostly between about 700 and 500 BC. They are called "Homeric" because they use Homer's metre and dialect, not because Homer wrote them. Most were probably sung as preludes before longer recitations of epic.

The four long hymns are substantial narrative poems. The *Hymn to Demeter* tells how Hades carried off Persephone, how her mother's grief made the crops fail, and how the pomegranate seeds Persephone ate bound her to return to the underworld each year; it is the founding myth of the Mysteries at Eleusis. The *Hymn to Apollo* tells of the god's birth on Delos and his founding of the oracle at Delphi. The *Hymn to Hermes* is a comedy in which the newborn god steals Apollo's cattle, invents the lyre and talks his way out of trouble. The *Hymn to Aphrodite* tells of the goddess's affair with the mortal Anchises, father of Aeneas.

Because they were composed over two centuries and in different places, the hymns are valuable evidence for how particular cults and sanctuaries presented their gods in the Archaic period.

The collection survives only in late medieval manuscripts; the Hymn to Demeter was known from a single copy found in Moscow in 1777.

name: The fragments of Sappho
author: Sappho
survival: One near-complete poem; c. 200 fragments, many from papyri

claims.text: Only one poem by Sappho survives essentially complete.
Much of the surviving corpus was recovered from Egyptian papyri.
Fragment 31 describes physical symptoms of desire and was widely imitated.
The loss of her work resulted mainly from changing transmission rather than deliberate destruction.
Recently published fragments are of secure provenance.

milestones.text: Dionysius of Halicarnassus quotes the Hymn to Aphrodite in full, the only complete poem to survive.
Papyri from the rubbish dumps of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt begin to yield new fragments.
A papyrus in Cologne completes the 'Tithonus poem' on old age.
The 'Brothers Poem' is published; questions about the papyrus's provenance follow.

summary: The surviving remains of nine books of lyric poetry — the most celebrated love poetry of antiquity, in pieces.
significance: The most celebrated love poetry of the ancient world, and the first great body of verse in a personal, lyric voice by a woman.
body:
The poems of Sappho of Lesbos, composed around 610–570 BC in her local Aeolic dialect for singing to the lyre. Ancient scholars gathered them into nine books — perhaps 10,000 lines. About 650 survive, mostly in fragments.

Only the *Hymn to Aphrodite* is essentially complete: a prayer in which the goddess comes down smiling and asks, with some amusement, who Sappho has fallen for this time. Fragment 31 describes watching a beloved woman talk and laugh with a man — the tongue breaks, fire runs under the skin, ears ring — and has been imitated from Catullus onward. Other fragments speak of weddings, family, memory and the women of her circle.

The poems were lost not mainly through deliberate destruction but because Aeolic dialect fell out of the school curriculum, and texts that stopped being copied disappeared. What survives comes from quotations by later ancient writers and from papyrus scraps recovered from the rubbish dumps of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt.

New texts are still appearing: the "Tithonus poem" was completed in 2004, and the "Brothers Poem" published in 2014, though questions have since been raised about how that papyrus was acquired.

name: The Histories
author: Herodotus

claims.text: The Histories investigates the causes of the Greco-Persian Wars.
Herodotus distinguishes explicitly between reporting and believing his sources.
Several of his ethnographic descriptions have been confirmed archaeologically.
His army and casualty figures are systematically exaggerated.
He personally visited all the regions he describes.

milestones.text: The oldest complete manuscript is the Florentine Laurentianus 70.3; papyri from Egypt preserve older fragments.
Lorenzo Valla's Latin translation is printed, bringing Herodotus to Western readers.
First printed in Greek by Aldus Manutius in Venice.

summary: An enquiry into why Greeks and Persians went to war, which becomes an account of the whole known world.
significance: The first work of history in the Western tradition, and the main source for the Persian Wars and for much of the 6th-century Mediterranean world.
body:
A prose history in the Ionic dialect, written by Herodotus of Halicarnassus between about 440 and 425 BC and later divided into nine books. Its stated aim is to preserve the great deeds of Greeks and non-Greeks from being forgotten, and to explain why they went to war with one another.

The first half ranges across the known world as the Persian Empire expands: the fall of Croesus of Lydia, the customs of Egypt, Babylon and the Scythians, and the rise of Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius. The second half narrates the Ionian Revolt and the Persian invasions of Greece — Marathon in 490 BC, then Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 BC.

Herodotus is open about his method. He names his informants where he can, gives competing versions side by side, and says repeatedly that he must report what he was told but need not believe it. Ancient critics called him "the father of lies", yet archaeology has confirmed many of his specific details, from Scythian burial customs to the canal Xerxes cut through the Athos peninsula. His weakness is numbers: the Persian armies he describes are far too large to be credible.

Cicero called him "the father of history", and the word *historia*, his "enquiry", gave the discipline its name.

name: History of the Peloponnesian War
author: Thucydides
survival: Incomplete; breaks off mid-sentence in book eight

claims.text: Thucydides excluded divine causation from his historical explanation.
The work breaks off unfinished in 411 BC.
He states that the speeches represent what was appropriate rather than verbatim record.
He was an eyewitness to the plague and an Athenian commander.
His account is free of Athenian bias.

milestones.text: The oldest complete manuscripts are Byzantine copies of the 10th and 11th centuries.
First printed in Greek by Aldus Manutius in Venice.
Thomas Hobbes publishes the first English translation made directly from the Greek.

summary: The war between Athens and Sparta, analysed without gods, omens or consolation — the founding work of critical history.
significance: The founding work of critical, evidence-based history, and still the main source for the war that ended Athens' empire.
body:
A prose history in eight books by the Athenian Thucydides, written from the outbreak of the war between Athens and Sparta in 431 BC until about 400 BC. Thucydides was himself an Athenian general; exiled in 424 BC after failing to save Amphipolis, he spent twenty years gathering testimony from both sides.

He sets out his method in deliberate contrast to Herodotus: no myths or marvels, eyewitness accounts checked against each other, and a work meant not to entertain but to be "a possession for all time". He explains events through human motives and power, never the gods. The war's real cause, he argues, was the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta.

Its best-known passages are analyses of power and its effects: Pericles' Funeral Oration for the Athenian dead; the plague of 430 BC, which Thucydides caught and survived; the civil war at Corcyra, where words changed meaning under factional violence; and the Melian Dialogue, in which Athenian envoys tell a small neutral island that "the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must". The speeches are his own reconstructions of what each situation required, a practice historians still debate.

The work breaks off mid-sentence in 411 BC, seven years before the war ended; Xenophon's *Hellenica* continues the story.

name: The Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
survival: Complete trilogy — the only one to survive

claims.text: The Oresteia is the only complete Greek tragic trilogy to survive.
It was produced in 458 BC and won first prize.
It stages the replacement of blood vengeance by a civic court.
It engages with contemporary reforms of the Areopagus.
A fourth, satyr play, Proteus, originally completed the tetralogy but does not survive.

milestones.text: The Medicean manuscript (Laurentianus 32.9) is the oldest copy; it alone preserves most of the Libation Bearers.
First printed by the Aldine press in Venice.

summary: Three plays tracing a cycle of blood vengeance to its end in the first court of law.
significance: The only complete Greek tragic trilogy to survive, and drama's founding story of justice passing from private revenge to public law.
body:
A trilogy of tragedies by Aeschylus, staged at the festival of Dionysus in Athens in 458 BC, where it won first prize. A fourth, comic satyr play, *Proteus*, completed the set but is lost.

In *Agamemnon*, the king returns from Troy and is murdered in his bath by his wife Clytemnestra, avenging their daughter Iphigenia, whom he sacrificed to win a wind for the fleet. In *The Libation Bearers*, their son Orestes returns from exile and, on Apollo's orders, kills his mother, and is driven mad by the Furies, goddesses who punish the shedding of kindred blood. In *The Eumenides*, Orestes is tried at Athens before a jury of citizens with Athena presiding. The vote is tied; Athena acquits him, and persuades the Furies to accept a new home in Athens as honoured guardians, the "Kindly Ones".

The trilogy dramatises the end of an endless chain of killing, replaced by a court whose verdict all sides accept. The court is the Areopagus, which had just been stripped of most of its political powers in the reforms of 462 BC, so the play spoke directly to a live and divisive question in the city.

It survives in the Medicean manuscript in Florence, and has been restaged and adapted constantly since the Renaissance.

name: Oedipus Rex
author: Sophocles

claims.text: Aristotle treated Oedipus Rex as the model of tragic plot construction.
The play uses sustained dramatic irony based on audience foreknowledge.
It did not win first prize on its original production.
Its opening plague reflects the real plague of Athens in the 420s BC.
Sigmund Freud named the Oedipus complex after the play, permanently shaping later popular readings of it.

milestones.text: The oldest manuscript is the Laurentianus 32.9 in Florence, which also contains Aeschylus.
First printed with Sophocles' other surviving plays by Aldus Manutius in Venice.

summary: A king investigating a plague discovers that he is himself the cause — the most tightly constructed plot in Greek drama.
significance: Held up by Aristotle as the model tragedy, and the most famous plot in Greek drama: a man who solves every riddle except the one about himself.
body:
A tragedy by Sophocles, first staged in Athens around 429–425 BC. Its opening, with Thebes dying of plague, may echo the plague that struck Athens in 430 BC, though that link is unproven.

The oracle at Delphi declares that the plague will lift only when the killer of the former king, Laius, is found and expelled. King Oedipus, who once saved Thebes by answering the riddle of the Sphinx, leads the investigation himself. Step by step — through the blind prophet Teiresias, his wife Jocasta and a messenger who arrives to reassure him — he discovers that he is the killer, that Laius was his father, and that Jocasta is his mother. Jocasta hangs herself and Oedipus blinds himself.

The audience knew the myth, so every confident word Oedipus speaks carries a meaning he cannot see: he curses the unknown killer, and so curses himself. Aristotle's *Poetics* treats the play as the ideal tragedy, above all for the moment when reversal of fortune and recognition of the truth arrive together. Its subject is less forbidden desire than knowledge: Oedipus is destroyed by finding out what he has already done.

The play reportedly did not win first prize. Freud's naming of the "Oedipus complex" after it has shaped popular readings ever since.

name: Antigone
author: Sophocles

claims.text: Antigone stages a conflict between religious obligation and civic decree.
It was produced around 441 BC.
Sophocles presents both Antigone and Creon as partly justified.
The play has been repeatedly adapted as political resistance literature.

milestones.text: The oldest manuscript is the Laurentianus 32.9 in Florence, which also contains Aeschylus.
First printed with Sophocles' other surviving plays by Aldus Manutius in Venice.

summary: A woman buries her brother against the king's edict — the founding text of the conflict between conscience and law.
significance: The classic statement of conscience against the law of the state, and one of the most adapted plays ever written.
body:
A tragedy by Sophocles, first staged in Athens around 441 BC. It continues the story of Oedipus' family after his sons Eteocles and Polynices have killed each other fighting for the throne of Thebes.

Creon, the new king, forbids burial for Polynices, who led a foreign army against his own city. His sister Antigone buries him anyway, appealing to the unwritten laws of the gods above any human decree. Creon has her walled up alive in a rock tomb. When he finally relents, it is too late: Antigone has hanged herself, Creon's son Haemon, who was to marry her, kills himself beside her, and Creon's wife then takes her own life. Creon is left alive with nothing.

The philosopher Hegel read the play as a clash not of right against wrong but of right against right. Creon defends the city's need for law and order; Antigone defends family and religious duty. Each holds to an absolute position, and each destroys what they care about.

The play has been reworked again and again as a drama of resistance to tyranny. Jean Anouilh's version, staged in occupied Paris in 1944, was ambiguous enough to be claimed by both the Resistance and the collaborationist authorities.

name: Medea
author: Euripides

claims.text: Medea was produced in 431 BC and placed third in the competition.
It contains an extended speech on the condition of married women.
Medea escapes without punishment at the end of the play.
Euripides invented the version in which Medea kills her own children.

milestones.text: Survives among the plays of Euripides selected for reading in Byzantine schools.
First printed in Florence by Janus Lascaris, with three other plays of Euripides.

summary: A foreign woman, abandoned by the husband she made a king, takes a revenge that destroys her own children.
significance: The most disturbing of Greek tragedies, and the sharpest ancient statement of a wife's and a foreigner's powerlessness.
body:
A tragedy by Euripides, first staged in Athens in 431 BC, the year the Peloponnesian War began. It placed third of three in the competition.

Medea, a princess from Colchis on the Black Sea, helped Jason win the Golden Fleece, betraying her father and killing her brother to do it. Now living with him in Corinth, she learns that Jason is setting her aside to marry the king's daughter, and that she and their two sons are to be exiled. Medea poisons the princess and her father with a gift of a robe and crown, then kills her own children to destroy Jason completely. She escapes in a chariot sent by her grandfather, the Sun. She is neither punished nor repentant; the play ends with Jason ruined below her.

Its most famous speech has Medea tell the women of Corinth what marriage means for a wife: bought with a dowry into a stranger's house, unable to leave, and told she lives safely at home while men face danger in war. She would rather stand in battle three times, she says, than give birth once. Whether Euripides invented the child-murder or took it from an earlier version is debated.

The play has become a touchstone in modern theatre for questions of gender, exile and revenge.

name: The Republic
author: Plato

claims.text: The Republic constructs an ideal city to investigate the nature of justice in the soul.
It advocates rule by philosopher-kings and censorship of poetry.
It argues that women should be eligible for guardianship and education.
Plato intended it as a practical political programme.
The dialogue's central image, the Allegory of the Cave, has become one of the most widely cited metaphors in Western philosophy.

milestones.text: The oldest surviving copy is the Byzantine manuscript Parisinus graecus 1807.
Marsilio Ficino's Latin translation of Plato is printed in Florence.
First printed in Greek, with Plato's other works, by Aldus Manutius in Venice.

summary: A dialogue that builds an ideal city in order to answer a question about the individual soul: is it better to be just?
significance: The most influential work of Western political philosophy: the source of the philosopher-king, the theory of Forms and the Allegory of the Cave.
body:
A dialogue in ten books by Plato, written in Athens around 380–375 BC, with Socrates as the main speaker. It asks whether it is better to be just than unjust, even if injustice could go undetected — the question Glaucon poses with the story of a ring that makes its wearer invisible.

To answer it, Socrates designs an ideal city, on the idea that justice will be easier to see written large in a state than in a single soul. The city is ruled by philosopher-kings, trained for decades and kept from private property and family life. Poetry, including Homer, is censored; rulers may tell a "noble lie" to keep citizens in their classes. Strikingly for its time, it argues that women should receive the same education and hold the same offices as men. The just soul, like the just city, is one in which reason rules over spirit and appetite.

The dialogue also contains Plato's theory of Forms and the Allegory of the Cave, in which prisoners mistake shadows on a wall for reality until one is led out into the sunlight. Whether the ideal city is a serious political programme or a thought experiment is debated; critics such as Karl Popper read it as a blueprint for authoritarian rule.

Its oldest surviving copy is a 9th-century Byzantine manuscript in Paris.

name: Poetics
author: Aristotle

claims.text: The Poetics analyses tragedy in terms of six constituent parts, with plot primary.
It introduces the concepts of hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis and catharsis.
The book dealing with comedy is lost.
Catharsis means the purgation of emotion rather than intellectual clarification.
Aristotle treats Sophocles' Oedipus Rex as the model of ideal tragic plot construction.

milestones.text: Translated into Arabic from a Syriac version; the Arabic preserves readings lost from the Greek.
The main Greek witness is the Byzantine manuscript Parisinus graecus 1741.
First printed in Greek by Aldus Manutius in Venice; its influence on Renaissance drama follows.

summary: The founding work of literary criticism, which analyses tragedy as a mechanism and asks what it does to an audience.
significance: The founding work of literary criticism, whose vocabulary of plot, reversal, recognition and catharsis is still the starting point for discussing drama.
body:
A short treatise by Aristotle, probably written as lecture notes in Athens around 335–323 BC. It survives incomplete: a second book, on comedy, is lost.

Aristotle treats poetry as a craft that can be analysed. Tragedy imitates a serious action through six parts — plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle — and plot matters most, since character exists for the sake of the action, not the reverse. He names the key moments of a tragic plot: *peripeteia*, the reversal of fortune; *anagnorisis*, recognition of the truth; and *hamartia*, the error that brings down a good person. Tragedy, he says, achieves *catharsis* of pity and fear, a word he never defines and which critics have argued over ever since. His constant example of excellence is Sophocles' *Oedipus Rex*.

He also argues that poetry is more philosophical than history, because history tells what happened while poetry shows what would happen — the universal rather than the particular. The treatise was in part an answer to Plato, who had banished poets from his ideal city.

Transmitted through Arabic as well as Greek and printed in 1508, it shaped Renaissance and neoclassical drama, and its lost book on comedy is the premise of Umberto Eco's *The Name of the Rose*.

name: Nicomachean Ethics
author: Aristotle

claims.text: The Ethics identifies eudaimonia as the human good and defines virtue as a mean between extremes.
It holds that virtue is acquired through habituation rather than instruction alone.
Two of its ten books are devoted to friendship.
It is the founding text of the virtue-ethics tradition.
The work is named after Aristotle's son Nicomachus, who is traditionally credited with editing or transmitting it.

milestones.text: Robert Grosseteste makes the first complete Latin translation, which shapes medieval moral philosophy.
First printed in Greek in Aldus Manutius' edition of Aristotle.

summary: An investigation of how to live well, arguing that virtue is a skill acquired by practice rather than a rule to be learned.
significance: The founding text of virtue ethics, and for centuries the most studied work of moral philosophy in Europe and the Islamic world.
body:
A treatise in ten books by Aristotle, based on his lectures at the Lyceum in Athens around 340–322 BC. Its name probably refers to his son Nicomachus, traditionally said to have edited it.

It asks how to live well. Everyone agrees, Aristotle says, that the goal is *eudaimonia* — flourishing — but not on what that is. His answer is a life of activity in accordance with virtue, over a complete lifetime. A virtue is a settled disposition lying in a mean between excess and deficiency, relative to the person and the situation: courage between recklessness and cowardice, generosity between waste and meanness. It cannot be reduced to rules, and it is learned by practice: we become just by doing just acts, as we become builders by building.

The work also analyses responsibility, weakness of will and practical wisdom, and gives two whole books to friendship, distinguishing friendships of usefulness, of pleasure and of good character. It ends by ranking the contemplative life of the philosopher highest of all.

Translated into Latin in the 13th century, it became central to medieval moral philosophy through Thomas Aquinas. Since the mid-20th century, virtue ethics built on it has again become a major position in philosophy.

name: The Philippics
author: Demosthenes

claims.text: Demosthenes delivered a series of speeches against Philip II between 351 and 341 BC.
He argued that Athens must fund and serve in campaigns directly rather than rely on mercenaries.
The term "philippic" became a generic name for a denunciatory speech.
The published speeches match what was actually delivered.
Demosthenes also delivered a related series of speeches, the Olynthiacs, urging Athenian support for the city of Olynthus against Philip.

milestones.text: Survives in Byzantine manuscripts of Demosthenes' collected speeches.
First printed in Greek by Aldus Manutius in Venice.

summary: Speeches warning Athens that Philip of Macedon was an existential threat — the finest Greek oratory, and unheeded.
significance: The most admired speeches of Greek oratory, and Athens' clearest warning of the Macedonian conquest that ended its independence.
body:
Four speeches delivered to the Athenian Assembly by the orator Demosthenes between 351 and 341 BC, as Philip II of Macedon expanded into northern Greece. A related set, the *Olynthiacs*, urged help for the city of Olynthus, which Philip destroyed in 348 BC.

Demosthenes' argument is consistent across a decade. Philip is not an ordinary rival who can be managed by treaties, but an opponent who campaigns in winter, uses bribery and mercenaries, and will take everything unless resisted now. He attacks the Athenians themselves for complacency: they wander the marketplace asking each other for news of Philip, and vote for expeditions they do not serve in. Athens, he urges, must pay for its wars and fight them with its own citizens.

The warnings largely failed. Athens built an alliance too late, and Philip defeated it at Chaeronea in 338 BC, ending the independence of the Greek city-states. Whether the published texts match what was actually said is uncertain.

As models of persuasion the speeches were studied for two thousand years. Cicero named his own attacks on Mark Antony *Philippics*, and the word still means a bitter denunciation.

name: Anabasis of Alexander
author: Arrian of Nicomedia

claims.text: Arrian based his account principally on Ptolemy and Aristobulus, both eyewitnesses.
Both of his principal sources are otherwise lost.
His military description is generally regarded as the most reliable of the Alexander historians.
His account is favourable to Alexander.
Arrian also wrote a separate, shorter work, the Indica, describing India and Nearchus's voyage back from the Indus.

milestones.text: Every surviving copy descends from a single damaged medieval manuscript in Vienna, with a gap in Book 7.
First printed in Greek in Venice.

summary: The most reliable surviving account of Alexander's campaigns, written four centuries later from participants' memoirs.
significance: The most reliable surviving narrative of Alexander's campaigns, and the main window onto the lost eyewitness accounts of his officers.
body:
A history of Alexander the Great's campaigns in seven books, written in Greek around AD 145–160 by Arrian of Nicomedia, a Greek from Asia Minor who held high office in the Roman Empire, including the governorship of Cappadocia. The title, "the march up-country", deliberately echoes Xenophon's *Anabasis*.

Arrian built his account on two eyewitnesses: Ptolemy, Alexander's general and later king of Egypt, and Aristobulus, an engineer on the expedition. Both works are lost, so Arrian is our access to them. He follows the campaign from Alexander's accession in 336 BC through the battles of the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, the march into Central Asia and India, the return through the Gedrosian desert and the king's death at Babylon in 323 BC.

Arrian had commanded troops himself, and his descriptions of formations, sieges and terrain are the most credible of any ancient Alexander historian. Where his sources disagree he says so, and he separates what is reported from what he believes. He is not neutral: he admires Alexander and treats the killing of Cleitus and the execution of Parmenion as lapses rather than as evidence of character.

A companion work, the *Indica*, describes India and the voyage of Alexander's admiral Nearchus from the Indus to the Persian Gulf.

name: Life of Alexander
author: Plutarch

claims.text: Plutarch explicitly distinguishes biography from history in his stated method.
The Life of Alexander is paired with the Life of Julius Caesar.
Plutarch preserves anecdotes from sources now lost.
Shakespeare drew directly on translations of Plutarch for several plays.

milestones.text: First printed in Greek with the other Parallel Lives in Florence.
Thomas North's English version, made from Jacques Amyot's French, becomes a source for Shakespeare.

summary: A biography paired with Julius Caesar, explicitly interested in character rather than military narrative.
significance: The source of most of the famous stories about Alexander, from Bucephalus to the Gordian knot, and the portrait of his character that later ages inherited.
body:
A biography of Alexander the Great by Plutarch of Chaeronea, written around AD 100–120 as part of his *Parallel Lives*, where it is paired with the life of Julius Caesar. Plutarch wrote more than four centuries after Alexander's death, drawing on many sources now lost.

He states his method at the start: he is writing lives, not histories, and a small thing — a phrase or a joke — often reveals character better than a battle in which thousands die. So the Life follows Alexander from his birth and education under Aristotle through his campaigns, but lingers on telling episodes: the boy taming the horse Bucephalus by turning it away from its own shadow; the cutting of the Gordian knot; the visit to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa; the drunken killing of his friend Cleitus and the remorse that followed; the final illness at Babylon.

Plutarch moralises and does not always separate anecdote from evidence, so historians use him alongside Arrian's more military account. But he preserves material found nowhere else, and his interest in character gives a portrait Arrian does not attempt.

Through Thomas North's English translation of 1579, Plutarch's Lives became a source for Shakespeare and a primer of ancient character for European readers.

name: Parallel Lives
author: Plutarch

claims.text: Parallel Lives pairs Greek and Roman figures with explicit comparisons.
Plutarch states a moral rather than historical purpose.
The work preserves material from sources now lost.
It was a major influence on Renaissance and Enlightenment political thought.

milestones.text: First printed in Greek in Florence.
Jacques Amyot's French translation makes the Lives a European bestseller.
Thomas North's English version, made from Amyot, becomes Shakespeare's source for his Roman plays.

summary: Fifty biographies pairing a Greek with a Roman, comparing their characters — the main channel through which antiquity reached Renaissance Europe.
significance: The main channel through which Renaissance and early modern Europe came to know the great figures of Greece and Rome.
body:
A collection of biographies by Plutarch of Chaeronea, a Greek writing under the Roman Empire around AD 100–120. Forty-eight lives survive, most of them in pairs that set a Greek beside a Roman: Theseus and Romulus, Lycurgus and Numa, Alexander and Caesar, Demosthenes and Cicero. Many pairs end with a short comparison.

Plutarch's aim is moral, not historical. He wants readers to measure their own conduct against these examples of virtue and vice, and chooses anecdotes that reveal character. The pairing also made a point to his own time: Greek history could stand as an equal beside Rome's.

Because he had access to libraries now lost, Plutarch is often the only source for particular events, people and earlier works. For figures such as Lycurgus, Solon and Pericles his Lives are among the fullest ancient accounts, though historians read them critically, as moral portraits written centuries after the fact.

Translated into French by Jacques Amyot (1559) and into English by Thomas North (1579), the Lives were read across Europe. Shakespeare took the plots of *Julius Caesar*, *Antony and Cleopatra* and *Coriolanus* from North, sometimes almost word for word, and revolutionaries in France and America read Plutarch as a handbook of public virtue.

name: Bibliotheca historica
author: Diodorus Siculus

claims.text: The Bibliotheca is a universal history compiled in the 1st century BC.
Books 11–20 survive complete and cover 480–302 BC.
It preserves material from historians whose works are otherwise lost.
Its chronology and internal consistency are unreliable.

milestones.text: Only 15 of its 40 books survive whole; the rest are known from Byzantine excerpts.
Books 16–20 are first printed in Greek in Basel.

summary: A universal history from mythical times to Caesar, valuable chiefly because it copies sources that no longer exist.
significance: Not a great history, but an indispensable one: for long stretches, especially the wars after Alexander, it is the only continuous narrative that survives.
body:
A universal history in 40 books, compiled in Greek by Diodorus of Sicily between about 60 and 30 BC. It runs from the mythical past to Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul. Books 1–5 and 11–20 survive whole; the rest are known from fragments and Byzantine excerpts.

Diodorus arranged events year by year, weaving Greek, Near Eastern, Sicilian and Roman history into one timeline — an ambitious attempt to treat the whole known world's past as a single story. The early books cover Egypt, Mesopotamia, India and Greek myth; Books 11–20 give a continuous narrative of 480–302 BC, from Xerxes' invasion through Philip II and Alexander to the wars of Alexander's successors.

As a historian he is a compiler rather than an analyst. He follows one source at a time, so he can contradict himself between books, and his dates are often wrong. His value lies in what he copied: for the wars of the Diadochi he follows Hieronymus of Cardia, a participant whose own history is lost, and for Philip II he draws on Ephorus and Theopompus, also lost. Reading Diodorus means reading through him to those better sources.

This is a common pattern in ancient history: the best writers vanish, and the compilations that copied them survive.

name: The Histories
author: Polybius
survival: Books 1–5 complete; the rest in excerpts

claims.text: Polybius set out to explain Roman expansion between 220 and 167 BC.
Book 6 analyses the Roman constitution as a mixed form with mutual checks.
He argued that historians require practical political and military experience.
His constitutional analysis influenced later republican political theory.
Polybius was held as a political hostage in Rome for around seventeen years, during which he became close to the Scipio family.

milestones.text: Only Books 1–5 survive complete; the rest of the 40 books are known from Byzantine excerpts.
First printed in Greek at Haguenau.
Isaac Casaubon's edition and Latin translation establish Polybius for early modern readers.

summary: An analysis of how Rome conquered the Mediterranean in fifty-three years, by a Greek who watched it from inside.
significance: The fullest ancient analysis of how Rome came to rule the Mediterranean, by a Greek who saw it happen; its theory of the mixed constitution influenced modern republics.
body:
A history in 40 books by Polybius of Megalopolis, written in Greek around 160–130 BC. Books 1–5 survive complete; the rest are known from long excerpts. Polybius was a leading Achaean politician who, after Rome's victory at Pydna in 168 BC, was deported to Italy as one of a thousand hostages. In Rome he became a close friend of Scipio Aemilianus, and later witnessed the destruction of Carthage and Corinth in 146 BC.

His question is how, and through what kind of constitution, Rome brought almost the whole known world under its rule in less than 53 years, from 220 to 167 BC. He narrates the Second Punic War with Hannibal and Rome's wars against Macedon and the Seleucids, including the classic comparison of the flexible Roman legion with the Macedonian phalanx.

Book 6 gives his answer: Rome's constitution mixes monarchy (the consuls), aristocracy (the Senate) and democracy (the popular assemblies), each checking the others, which slows the cycle of decline that destroys simpler constitutions. Polybius also insists that historians need practical political and military experience, must visit the places they describe and question participants.

His idea of a balanced constitution passed through Montesquieu to the framers of the United States Constitution.

name: The Elements
author: Euclid

claims.text: The Elements derives geometrical results from a small set of stated postulates.
It includes a proof that the primes are infinite in number.
It remained a standard mathematics textbook into the 20th century.
The parallel postulate is logically independent of the other four.

milestones.text: Translated into Arabic in Baghdad; Arabic versions carry it through the Islamic world.
The oldest dated Greek copy, now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS D'Orville 301).
First printed, in Campanus' Latin version, by Erhard Ratdolt in Venice.
First printed in Greek in Basel.

summary: Thirteen books deriving all of Greek geometry from five postulates — the most successful textbook ever written.
significance: The most successful textbook ever written: for over two thousand years, the model of how to prove something from first principles.
body:
A mathematical work in thirteen books, written in Greek by Euclid at Alexandria around 300 BC, early in the reign of Ptolemy I. Little is known of Euclid himself.

The *Elements* gathers and organises the geometry and number theory of earlier Greek mathematicians into a single system. It begins with 23 definitions, five postulates and five common notions, and proves everything else from them, each step depending only on what has already been shown. Book I ends with Pythagoras' theorem; Book IX proves that there are infinitely many prime numbers; Book X deals with irrational magnitudes; Book XIII constructs the five regular solids and proves there are no others.

Its originality lies less in new results than in method: the idea that a whole body of knowledge can be derived by strict logic from a few stated assumptions. The fifth postulate, about parallel lines, was less obvious than the others, and two thousand years of attempts to prove it failed. In the 19th century Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Riemann showed that rejecting it produces consistent alternative geometries, one of which general relativity later required.

Translated into Arabic and Latin and first printed in 1482, it remained a standard school text into the 20th century.

name: Argonautica
author: Apollonius of Rhodes

claims.text: The Argonautica retells the voyage for the Golden Fleece in four books.
Book 3 gives an extended psychological portrait of Medea in love.
It directly influenced Virgil's treatment of Dido in the Aeneid.
Apollonius served as head of the Library of Alexandria.
Apollonius quarrelled with Callimachus over epic poetry.

milestones.text: The oldest manuscript is in the Laurentian Library, Florence, with ancient scholars' notes in the margins.
First printed in Florence by Janus Lascaris.

summary: Jason's voyage for the Golden Fleece, retold as a Hellenistic epic with a psychologically realistic heroine.
significance: The only Greek epic to survive between Homer and the Roman age, and the first long portrait of a mind in love — the model for Virgil's Dido.
body:
An epic in four books by Apollonius of Rhodes, written at Alexandria around 250–240 BC. Apollonius worked at the Ptolemies' court and, by ancient tradition, was head of the Library of Alexandria; his surname may reflect a later move to Rhodes.

It tells the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts to Colchis, at the far end of the Black Sea, to win the Golden Fleece. Book 1 gathers the heroes and sails, Book 2 takes them through the Clashing Rocks, Book 3 sets Jason his impossible tasks in Colchis, and Book 4 follows the long, roundabout journey home.

Apollonius wrote epic in an age that thought Homer could not be matched, and changed its emphasis. His Jason is often at a loss and succeeds largely through others. The real innovation is Book 3, which follows the princess Medea falling in love — sleepless, arguing with herself, deciding to betray her father for a stranger. It is the first extended inner portrait of a person in love in European literature. The poem is also full of Alexandrian learning: rare geography, explanations of local customs and allusions to earlier poets.

Virgil drew directly on Medea for Dido in the *Aeneid*. A later story of a feud between Apollonius and the poet Callimachus may be invented.

name: The Idylls
author: Theocritus

claims.text: Theocritus originated the pastoral genre in Greek poetry.
His pastoral world was written for an urban Alexandrian audience.
The Idylls directly influenced Virgil's Eclogues.
Some poems in the collection are not by Theocritus.

milestones.text: First printed in Milan, with Hesiod's Works and Days.
A fuller collection is printed by Aldus Manutius in Venice.

summary: Short poems of herdsmen singing in the Sicilian countryside — the invention of pastoral poetry.
significance: The invention of pastoral poetry, the tradition of shepherds singing in an idealised countryside that runs from Virgil to the English Romantics.
body:
About thirty short poems by Theocritus, a poet from Syracuse in Sicily who worked at Alexandria and on Kos around 275–260 BC. Some poems in the collection are by later imitators.

The best known are pastorals: goatherds and cowherds in the Sicilian countryside compete in song, mourn lost loves and lament the dead herdsman Daphnis. Theocritus wrote them in a stylised literary version of the Doric dialect spoken in Sicily, giving the poems a rustic flavour. But their audience was urban and educated, and the countryside they describe is a knowing literary fiction.

Not all the Idylls are rural. Some are short mythological narratives; others are urban mimes. Idyll 15 follows two Syracusan housewives through the crowded streets of Alexandria to a festival of Adonis at the palace, grumbling about their husbands and the crowds — one of the liveliest scenes of everyday city life in Greek literature. Others praise the poet's royal patron, Ptolemy II.

Virgil's *Eclogues* adapted the form for Latin. From there it ran through Renaissance pastoral, Milton's *Lycidas* and Shelley's *Adonais*, and the whole tradition of elegy set among shepherds.

name: The Septuagint
author: Jewish scholars at Alexandria

claims.text: The Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek at Alexandria beginning in the 3rd century BC.
The translation was produced gradually over roughly 150 years by multiple translators.
New Testament authors generally quote the Greek rather than the Hebrew text.
The account of seventy-two independent identical translations is legendary.
The Letter of Aristeas claims the translation was commissioned by Ptolemy II for the Library of Alexandria.

milestones.text: The oldest surviving Greek fragments, from Egypt and later from Qumran, date from within two centuries of the translation.
Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, the oldest near-complete Greek Bibles, are copied.
Constantin von Tischendorf finds the first leaves of Codex Sinaiticus at St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai.
First published in Greek by the Aldine press in Venice.
Greek fragments of the Old Testament are among the Dead Sea Scrolls found at Qumran.

summary: The Hebrew scriptures translated into Greek at Alexandria — the first major translation of a sacred text in history.
significance: The first great translation of a sacred text: it made Jewish scripture readable across the Greek-speaking world and became the Old Testament of the early Church.
body:
The Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, made by Jewish scholars at Alexandria between about 280 and 130 BC. The Torah was translated first, in the 3rd century BC, and the other books followed over the next 150 years, in markedly different translation styles.

Alexandria had a large Jewish community that increasingly spoke Greek, and it needed its scriptures in a language it could read. The *Letter of Aristeas*, written in the 2nd century BC, tells a grander story: King Ptolemy II asked for a copy of the Jewish law for the Library of Alexandria, and 72 scholars sent from Jerusalem produced it in 72 days — the source of the name "Septuagint", from the Latin for seventy. Later versions of the legend claimed the scholars worked separately and produced identical texts, a story meant to certify the translation as divinely guided.

Its influence was enormous. It made Jewish scripture available across the Hellenistic world, and the writers of the New Testament usually quote it rather than the Hebrew. Its word choices shaped Christian theology: where Isaiah's Hebrew speaks of a "young woman" (*almah*), the Greek has *parthenos*, "virgin".

It remains the Old Testament of the Greek Orthodox Church. Its oldest near-complete copies are the 4th-century AD Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus.

name: The Persians
author: Aeschylus

claims.text: The Persians was staged in 472 BC and won first prize; Pericles paid for its chorus.
It is the oldest surviving Greek tragedy and the only one on a recent historical event.
Aeschylus himself had fought against the Persians.

milestones.text: First printed with Aeschylus' other plays by the Aldine press in Venice.

summary: Aeschylus' tragedy of 472 BC about the Persian defeat at Salamis, told from the Persian court — the oldest surviving Greek play.
significance: The oldest surviving play in the Western tradition, and a rare tragedy about real recent events, written by a veteran of the war it portrays.
body:
*The Persians* was staged by Aeschylus at the City Dionysia in Athens in 472 BC, eight years after the battle of Salamis, and won first prize. The wealthy young Pericles paid for its chorus. It is the oldest Greek tragedy to survive, and the only surviving one that takes its subject not from myth but from recent history.

The play is set at the Persian royal court at Susa. The chorus of elders and the queen mother Atossa wait anxiously for news of Xerxes' invasion of Greece. A messenger arrives and describes the disaster at Salamis in a long, vivid speech, the earliest account of the battle. The ghost of Xerxes' father, Darius, is summoned from the tomb and blames his son's arrogance in bridging the Hellespont and offending the gods. Finally Xerxes himself enters in rags, and the play ends in a long lament.

Aeschylus had himself fought against the Persians, probably at Salamis as well as Marathon. Yet the play does not simply gloat. It shows the enemy's grief with sympathy and presents the defeat as a warning about *hubris*, the overconfidence that brings ruin — a lesson Athenians, already building an empire, might apply to themselves.

It is a key source for how Greeks saw the Persian Wars, and remains one of the most performed Greek plays.

name: Prometheus Bound
author: Attributed to Aeschylus
survival: Complete; the rest of its trilogy lost

claims.text: Prometheus Bound was transmitted under Aeschylus' name, but many scholars doubt his authorship.
It shows Prometheus chained to a rock as punishment for giving fire to humanity.
It was probably part of a trilogy, with a lost sequel, Prometheus Unbound.

summary: A tragedy in which the Titan Prometheus, chained to a rock by Zeus for giving fire to humans, defies the tyranny of the new king of the gods.
significance: The great drama of defiance against power, whose rebel Titan became a hero for Romantic poets and revolutionaries.
body:
*Prometheus Bound* has come down to us among the plays of Aeschylus, but its style and ideas have led many scholars to doubt that he wrote it; it may be the work of a follower, or his son, in the 440s or 430s BC. It was probably part of a trilogy whose other plays, including *Prometheus Unbound*, are lost.

The play opens as the gods Power and Force, with a reluctant Hephaestus, chain the Titan Prometheus to a rock in the remote Caucasus. His crime was to steal fire and give it to humans, against the will of Zeus, the new ruler of the gods. Prometheus, whose name means "forethought", lists the arts he has taught mankind — building, writing, numbers, medicine, sailing — and presents himself as humanity's benefactor.

He is visited by the chorus of sea nymphs, by the god Oceanus, who urges him to submit, and by Io, a mortal woman driven across the world by the jealousy of Hera. Prometheus knows a secret that threatens Zeus' rule and refuses to reveal it. When Hermes comes to demand it, he still refuses, and the play ends as Zeus hurls him into the abyss with thunder and earthquake.

Its portrait of Zeus as a harsh new tyrant has made the play a lasting image of resistance, and inspired Shelley's *Prometheus Unbound*.

name: The Bacchae
author: Euripides

claims.text: The Bacchae was written at the Macedonian court and staged after Euripides' death, winning first prize.
It is the only surviving tragedy with Dionysus as a central character.
In the play King Pentheus is torn apart by his mother Agave and the women of Thebes.

summary: Euripides' last tragedy, in which the god Dionysus takes terrible revenge on the king of Thebes who refuses to worship him.
significance: The only surviving tragedy about Dionysus, the god of the theatre itself, and one of the most powerful plays about religion and the irrational.
body:
Euripides wrote the *Bacchae* late in life at the court of King Archelaus of Macedon, where he died in 406 BC. His son staged it in Athens the following year, and it won first prize.

The god Dionysus arrives in Thebes disguised as a young man, bringing his ecstatic cult from Asia. His mother Semele was a Theban princess, but the city has denied that he is a god. He has driven the women of Thebes, among them King Pentheus' mother Agave, into the mountains, where as Bacchants they dance, handle snakes and tear animals apart with their bare hands. The young king Pentheus, rigid and hostile, tries to suppress the cult and imprisons the stranger, who escapes as the palace shakes.

Dionysus then plays on Pentheus' curiosity and lures him, dressed as a woman, to spy on the women. There they discover him and, in their frenzy, tear him limb from limb, with Agave leading them in the belief that he is a lion. She returns to the city carrying her son's head in triumph, and slowly realises what she has done.

The play shows both the joy and the terrible violence of the god of wine and ecstasy, the god in whose honour the play itself was performed. Its meaning — whether it celebrates or condemns Dionysus — is still debated.

name: The Trojan Women
author: Euripides

claims.text: The Trojan Women was staged in 415 BC, months after Athens destroyed Melos.
It shows the fate of the women of Troy after the city's fall.
Whether the play was intended as a protest against Athenian conduct at Melos is debated.

summary: Euripides' tragedy of 415 BC about the women of Troy awaiting slavery after the city's fall — one of the most powerful anti-war plays ever written.
significance: A stark portrait of the suffering war inflicts on the defeated, staged by Athens in the year it massacred the people of Melos.
body:
*The Trojan Women* was staged at the City Dionysia in Athens in 415 BC, as part of a set of plays on the Trojan War. A few months earlier, Athens had captured the neutral island of Melos, killed its men and enslaved its women and children, and it was about to launch the Sicilian Expedition.

The play has almost no plot. Troy has fallen, and its women wait by the shore to be shared out as slaves among the Greek victors. The aged queen Hecuba learns the fate of each of her family in turn. Her daughter Cassandra, given to Agamemnon, foresees his murder and her own. Hector's widow Andromache is to go to the son of the man who killed her husband, and her little son Astyanax is taken from her and thrown from the walls of Troy, for fear he will grow up to avenge his father; Hecuba buries him in his father's shield. Helen pleads for her life before her husband Menelaus. The play ends as Troy burns and the women are led to the ships.

The gods Poseidon and Athena, in the opening scene, plan to punish the Greeks on their voyage home, suggesting that the victors too will suffer. Whether Euripides meant the play as a protest against Melos is debated, but it has been revived many times as a protest against war.

name: The Clouds
author: Aristophanes

claims.text: The Clouds was first staged in 423 BC and placed third; the surviving text is a partly revised version.
It portrays Socrates as a sophist running a school called the Thinkery.
In Plato's Apology Socrates cites the play as a source of prejudice against him.

summary: Aristophanes' comedy of 423 BC mocking Socrates as a quack teacher of clever argument — a caricature remembered at his trial.
significance: The only contemporary portrait of Socrates by someone other than his followers, and a sharp satire of the new learning in Athens.
body:
*The Clouds* was first staged at the City Dionysia of 423 BC, where it came third of three. Aristophanes later partly revised it, and the version we have is this revision, which was probably never performed.

The old farmer Strepsiades is drowning in debts run up by his horse-mad son Pheidippides. He enrols at the "Thinkery" (*phrontistērion*) of Socrates, hoping to learn the "Worse Argument" that can win any case, so that he can cheat his creditors. Socrates is shown suspended in a basket, studying the heavens, worshipping the Clouds instead of Zeus, and teaching absurd science. Strepsiades is too stupid to learn, so he sends his son, who learns all too well: he beats his father and proves, by clever argument, that he was right to do so. In fury, Strepsiades burns down the Thinkery.

Aristophanes' Socrates is a caricature, mixing him with the natural philosophers and the paid Sophists, though the real Socrates took no fees. But the play shows how many Athenians saw the new learning — as a threat to religion, morality and the authority of fathers.

In Plato's *Apology*, Socrates tells the jury at his trial in 399 BC that the prejudice against him goes back to plays like this one, in which a "Socrates" swings around claiming to walk on air.

name: Lysistrata
author: Aristophanes

claims.text: Lysistrata was staged in 411 BC, after the Sicilian disaster.
In the play the women of Greece go on a sex strike and seize the Acropolis to force peace.
Its female roles were played by male actors.

summary: Aristophanes' comedy of 411 BC in which the women of Athens and Sparta end the war by refusing sex to their husbands.
significance: The most famous ancient comedy, and a wartime plea for peace among the Greeks that is still staged as an anti-war play.
body:
*Lysistrata* was staged in 411 BC, probably at the Lenaia festival, two years after the destruction of Athens' army in Sicily, when the Peloponnesian War was going badly and Athenian democracy was about to be overthrown by an oligarchic coup.

The Athenian woman Lysistrata, whose name means "disbander of armies", gathers women from across Greece, including the Spartan Lampito, and persuades them to swear an oath: they will refuse to sleep with their husbands until the men make peace. Meanwhile the older women seize the Acropolis, where the city's war treasury is kept. A chorus of old men tries to smoke them out and is drenched with water by a chorus of old women. The men, in increasing physical discomfort, grow desperate, and envoys from Sparta arrive in the same state. Lysistrata brings the two sides together, reminds them of their shared history against Persia, and a peace is celebrated with a feast and dancing.

It is a bawdy fantasy — in reality Athenian women had no political voice, and all the parts were played by men. But beneath the jokes lies a serious appeal to end a ruinous war between Greeks.

The play has been revived and adapted around the world, often in protest against war.

name: The Frogs
author: Aristophanes

claims.text: The Frogs won first prize at the Lenaia of 405 BC and was given a second performance.
In the play Dionysus judges a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides in the underworld.
It is the earliest surviving work of extended literary criticism in Greek.

summary: Aristophanes' comedy of 405 BC in which Dionysus goes down to Hades to bring back a great tragic poet, and judges a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides.
significance: A brilliant comedy and the first great work of literary criticism, staged as Athens faced defeat.
body:
*The Frogs* won first prize at the Lenaia festival in 405 BC, the year after the deaths of Euripides and Sophocles, and only months before Athens' final defeat in the Peloponnesian War. It was so admired that it was given a rare second performance.

Dionysus, god of the theatre, complains that there are no good tragic poets left, and sets off for the underworld to bring Euripides back, disguised as Heracles and accompanied by his slave Xanthias. He is rowed across the lake of the dead, accompanied by a chorus of croaking frogs, which gives the play its title, and meets a chorus of initiates of the Mysteries.

In Hades, Aeschylus and Euripides are quarrelling over who is the best tragedian. Dionysus judges a contest between them. They criticise each other's style, prologues and songs, and their verses are weighed on a pair of scales. Aeschylus is grand, old-fashioned and patriotic; Euripides clever, realistic and argumentative. In the end Dionysus asks them for advice to save the city, and chooses to bring Aeschylus back.

The play mixes slapstick with sharp comments on Athenian politics, including the famous comparison of good citizens with good coins driven out by bad. Its contest is the earliest extended piece of literary criticism in Greek.

name: The Apology of Socrates
author: Plato

claims.text: The Apology presents Socrates' speeches at his trial in 399 BC.
How closely it reproduces what Socrates actually said is uncertain.
In it Socrates says that the unexamined life is not worth living.

summary: Plato's account of Socrates' defence speech at his trial in 399 BC, and of his response to the death sentence.
significance: The founding portrait of the philosopher who dies rather than give up questioning — and the source of "the unexamined life is not worth living".
body:
The *Apology* (from the Greek *apologia*, "defence speech") was written by Plato some years after the trial of Socrates in 399 BC, which Plato attended. It presents three speeches by Socrates to the jury of 500 Athenian citizens. How closely it reproduces his actual words is unknown, but it is the fullest account of the trial; Xenophon wrote a shorter *Apology* of his own.

In the first speech Socrates answers the charges of impiety and corrupting the young. He says the prejudice against him comes partly from comedies such as Aristophanes' *Clouds*, and explains his way of life: when the oracle at Delphi said no one was wiser than him, he set out to test it by questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen, and found that his only wisdom was to know that he knew nothing. He cross-examines his accuser Meletus, and insists he will never stop practising philosophy, for "the unexamined life is not worth living".

Found guilty, he proposes, half seriously, that he should be given free meals at public expense as a benefactor of the city, then offers a fine of thirty minas. Condemned to death, he tells the jury that death is either a dreamless sleep or a journey to meet the great men of the past, and that no harm can come to a good man.

The *Apology* made Socrates the model of intellectual integrity.

name: The Symposium
author: Plato

claims.text: The Symposium is set at a drinking party in 416 BC celebrating the tragic poet Agathon's victory.
Its guests, including Aristophanes and Socrates, give speeches in praise of love (Eros).
Socrates presents a theory of love taught to him by a woman, Diotima of Mantinea.

summary: Plato's dialogue set at an Athenian drinking party, where the guests take turns praising love — the most famous work of philosophy on the subject.
significance: Plato's great work on love and beauty, the source of the idea of "Platonic love" and a vivid picture of Athenian intellectual life.
body:
Plato wrote the *Symposium* around 385–370 BC. It is set in 416 BC at a drinking party (*symposion*) held by the tragic poet Agathon to celebrate his first victory at the dramatic festival, and is told at second hand years later.

Instead of heavy drinking, the guests agree that each will give a speech in praise of Eros, the god of love. The speakers include Phaedrus, the doctor Eryximachus and the comic poet Aristophanes. Aristophanes tells a famous myth: humans were once double beings, with four arms and four legs, until Zeus split them in two, and ever since each half has searched for its other half; love is the longing to be whole again.

Socrates speaks last. He says he learned about love from a wise woman, Diotima of Mantinea. Love, she taught, is the desire for beauty and goodness, and can lead the soul upwards like a ladder: from love of one beautiful body, to all beautiful bodies, to beautiful souls, laws and knowledge, and finally to the vision of Beauty itself, eternal and unchanging.

Then the drunken Alcibiades bursts in and gives a speech praising Socrates himself — his self-control, his courage in battle and his strange power to move those who listen to him.

The dialogue gave the world the idea of "Platonic love" and remains one of Plato's most widely read works.

name: Politics
author: Aristotle

claims.text: In the Politics Aristotle calls the human being by nature a political animal (zoon politikon).
It classifies constitutions into rule by one, few and many, each with good and corrupt forms.
Aristotle defends slavery as natural for some people in Book 1.

summary: Aristotle's treatise on the city-state and its constitutions, the foundation of political science.
significance: The first systematic study of politics, which shaped political thought from the Middle Ages to the founders of modern republics.
body:
The *Politics*, in eight books, was written by Aristotle at the Lyceum in Athens, probably in the 330s and 320s BC, and is closely linked to his *Nicomachean Ethics*: ethics asks what the good life is, politics how a community can make it possible. It draws on the collection of 158 Greek constitutions made by Aristotle and his students.

Aristotle begins with the household and the village, and argues that the polis is the natural end of human association, existing "for the sake of the good life". The human being, he says, is by nature a political animal (*zōon politikon*): anyone who can live without a city is either a beast or a god. In the same first book he defends slavery, arguing that some people are slaves by nature, and the rule of men over women.

He then classifies constitutions by whether one, a few or many rule, and whether they rule for the common good or their own interest. The good forms are kingship, aristocracy and "polity"; their corrupt forms are tyranny, oligarchy and democracy. He argues that the most stable practical constitution is a mixed one resting on a strong middle class. He discusses the causes of revolution, and sketches an ideal city with careful education of its citizens.

Translated into Latin in the 13th century, the *Politics* became a founding text of Western political science.

name: Anabasis
author: Xenophon

claims.text: Xenophon's Anabasis narrates the expedition of Cyrus the Younger and the retreat of the Ten Thousand in 401–399 BC.
Xenophon took part in the expedition and became one of its leaders.
Ancient readers used it as a guide to Persia; Arrian modelled his history of Alexander on it.

summary: Xenophon's first-hand account of the Greek mercenaries who marched into Persia with Cyrus the Younger and fought their way home.
significance: The great eyewitness adventure story of antiquity, and a lesson to later Greeks — Alexander among them — that Persia could be crossed by a Greek army.
body:
The *Anabasis*, "The March Up-Country", was written by the Athenian Xenophon, probably in the 370s or 360s BC, decades after the events it describes. In seven books it tells the story of the expedition of 401–399 BC in which he took part.

Cyrus the Younger, brother of the Persian king Artaxerxes II, hired some 10,000 Greek mercenaries and led them from Sardis into Mesopotamia, at first concealing his aim to seize the throne. At Cunaxa near Babylon in 401 BC the Greeks won their part of the battle, but Cyrus was killed. When the Persians treacherously murdered their generals, Xenophon was elected one of the new leaders. The rest of the book follows their retreat north through the mountains of Kurdistan and Armenia in winter, harassed by enemies and weather, until they sighted the Black Sea and cried "The sea! The sea!"

Xenophon writes clearly and vividly, describing marches, battles, councils, foraging and the problems of leading an army of independent-minded Greeks. He writes about himself in the third person, presenting his own decisions in a favourable light.

The *Anabasis* was used in antiquity as a guide to Persia and to leadership; Arrian named his history of Alexander after it. For centuries it was a standard first Greek reading book for students.

name: The Hippocratic Corpus
author: Hippocrates and his school (various authors)

claims.text: The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of about 60 medical treatises by various authors, mostly of the late 5th and 4th centuries BC.
Which, if any, of the treatises were written by Hippocrates himself is unknown.
On the Sacred Disease argues that epilepsy has natural, not divine, causes.
The Hippocratic Oath binds doctors not to harm patients and to keep their confidences.

summary: The collection of some sixty Greek medical writings attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, the foundation of Western medicine.
significance: The first body of rational medicine, explaining disease by natural causes and setting the ethical ideals of doctors still invoked today.
body:
The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of about sixty medical treatises in Ionic Greek, attributed in antiquity to Hippocrates of Kos (c. 460–370 BC). In fact they were written by many authors, mostly in the late 5th and 4th centuries BC, and were probably gathered in the library at Alexandria. Which, if any, Hippocrates himself wrote is unknown.

The treatises cover the whole of medicine: anatomy, diet, surgery, fractures and dislocations, gynaecology, prognosis, epidemics and the effects of climate. Their central idea is that diseases have natural causes, such as diet, environment and the balance of the body's fluids, rather than being sent by gods. *On the Sacred Disease* argues that epilepsy is no more divine than any other illness. *Airs, Waters, Places* links health to climate and geography. The *Epidemics* record individual case histories in careful detail, including many patients who died. Several works developed the theory of four bodily "humours" — blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile — which dominated medicine for two thousand years.

The most famous text is the *Oath*, in which a new doctor swears by Apollo, Asclepius and the healing gods to help the sick and do them no harm, not to give poison, and to keep patients' secrets.

Through Galen in the Roman period, and later Arabic and Latin translations, the Hippocratic writings shaped medicine until modern times.

name: Aesop's Fables
author: Attributed to Aesop
survival: Several hundred fables in later collections

claims.text: Herodotus says Aesop was a slave on Samos in the 6th century BC.
The surviving fables come from later collections by writers such as Phaedrus and Babrius.
Socrates is said to have versified Aesop's fables in prison.

summary: Short moral tales of talking animals credited to Aesop, a slave storyteller of the 6th century BC.
significance: The most famous fables in the world — the tortoise and the hare, the fox and the grapes — and among the most widely read works of Greek origin.
body:
Aesop was a storyteller of the 6th century BC whom Herodotus describes as a slave on the island of Samos. Later legend made him an ugly but brilliant man from Thrace or Phrygia who won his freedom by his wit, advised kings such as Croesus, and was unjustly killed at Delphi. Almost nothing about him is certain, and he probably wrote nothing down.

Aesop's fables are short tales, usually about animals who talk and act like people, each ending in a lesson. The tortoise beats the boastful hare in a race; the fox, unable to reach the grapes, decides they are sour; the boy who cries "wolf" is not believed when the wolf really comes; the ant stores food for winter while the grasshopper sings. Such stories were part of everyday Greek culture: Aristophanes' characters quote them, and Plato says Socrates spent his last days in prison putting Aesop's fables into verse.

The fables were passed down orally and collected later. Demetrius of Phalerum made a collection around 300 BC, now lost. The surviving versions come from the Latin verse of Phaedrus in the 1st century AD, the Greek verse of Babrius, and later prose collections.

Aesop's fables became a standard school text in antiquity and the Middle Ages, and were retold by La Fontaine and countless others. Many of their lessons survive as proverbs.

name: Pindar's Victory Odes
author: Pindar

claims.text: Pindar's 45 surviving victory odes celebrate winners at the Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean Games.
The odes were commissioned by victors or their families and performed by choruses.
His datable odes run from 498 to 446 BC.

summary: The choral songs Pindar composed to celebrate victors at the four great Panhellenic games, the summit of Greek lyric poetry.
significance: The greatest surviving Greek choral poetry, and a window on the values of the athletic aristocracy of the early Classical age.
body:
Pindar of Thebes (c. 518–438 BC) was the most celebrated lyric poet of ancient Greece. Of his many works, four books of *epinikia*, or victory odes, survive almost complete — 45 poems arranged by the games they celebrate: Olympian, Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean. The datable odes run from 498 to 446 BC.

A victory ode was commissioned by the winner, his family or his city, and performed by a chorus with music and dance, either at the games or at a celebration back home. Pindar's patrons included the tyrants Hieron of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas, kings of Cyrene and Macedon, and aristocratic families from across the Greek world.

The odes rarely describe the race itself. Instead they set the victory in the light of the gods and of myth, praising the victor's family and city, and linking his success to the heroes of the past. They combine a myth — such as Pelops' chariot race in *Olympian* 1 or the founding of Cyrene in *Pythian* 4 — with prayers, moral sayings and reflections on human fortune: "Creatures of a day! What is a man? What is he not? A dream of a shadow is man."

Pindar's language is dense, allusive and soaring, and was admired and imitated in antiquity; Horace said that trying to rival him was like flying on wings of wax. He gave his name to the ode in European poetry.

name: Description of Greece
author: Pausanias

claims.text: Pausanias wrote the Description of Greece in ten books in the 2nd century AD.
It covers Attica, the Peloponnese, Boeotia and Phocis, region by region.
Its descriptions have repeatedly helped archaeologists identify buildings and works of art.

summary: Pausanias' ten-book guide to the sanctuaries, monuments and works of art of mainland Greece, written in the 2nd century AD.
significance: The most important guidebook of the ancient world, and an indispensable source for Greek art, religion and topography.
body:
The *Description of Greece* was written by Pausanias in the mid-2nd century AD, under the Roman emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius. In ten books it describes mainland Greece region by region: Attica and Megara, Corinth and the Argolid, Laconia, Messenia, Elis and Olympia (two books), Achaea, Arcadia, Boeotia and Phocis with Delphi.

Pausanias travelled along the main roads, describing what he saw: temples, altars, tombs, statues and paintings, and the myths, local histories and religious customs connected with them. He was interested above all in the past of Greece before the Romans, and passed over most recent buildings. His accounts of the Acropolis of Athens, the sanctuaries of Olympia and Delphi, the Statue of Zeus by Pheidias and the ruins of Mycenae are among the fullest that survive.

Modern scholars once dismissed him as a dull compiler of second-hand information. Archaeology has proved him a careful and accurate observer: excavators at Olympia, Delphi and Athens have used his descriptions to identify buildings and statues, and Schliemann used him at Mycenae. Many works of art are known only from his descriptions.

The book was rediscovered in the Renaissance and printed in 1516, and has been the guide of travellers to Greece ever since.
